topic_title: Christmas Window Painting Ideas: 10 Easy Designs to Copy
intro: Window painting works best when the design reads from the street, so bold outlines and a few strong colors beat fine detail. Paint on the inside of the glass if you want it to survive rain, and remember the design will be seen in reverse from outside, which matters for lettering. Clean the glass with plain water first, since spray cleaners can leave a film that makes paint bead. Sketch the layout with a white chalk marker before filling in color, and keep large areas for the corners and edges so the view stays open.

picks.description: Snowflakes are the most forgiving design for a first attempt because they are built from straight lines, and small wobbles read as natural variety. Start with a plus sign, cross it with an X, then add short V-shaped branches near the end of each arm. Cluster five to seven snowflakes of different sizes in the top corners and let a few drift toward the middle, which frames the view instead of blocking it. White liquid chalk markers give the crispest lines and show up well against a dark night sky; add a few in pale blue for depth. A white sponge dabbed along the bottom edge of the pane suggests a snowdrift and hides any uneven glass near the frame. The trade-off is that white designs fade into a bright winter day, so they look best after dark with indoor lights on.
picks.best_for: Beginners, rental windows and any room facing the street at night
picks.skip_if: Your window faces bright daylight all day and you want color that shows from far away
picks.quirky_fact: Real snowflakes almost always have six arms, so drawing eight-armed ones is the one detail people notice up close.
picks.product_name: Chalkola White Liquid Chalk Markers, Fine Tip

picks.breed: Painted Wreath With a Red Bow
picks.description: A painted wreath gives a front window the same welcome as a real one on the door, without hooks or needles. Trace a dinner plate or a large bowl with a chalk marker to get an even circle, then build the greenery with short, angled strokes of two greens in a ring about three inches wide. Dots of red for berries and a few gold circles for small ornaments break up the green. The bow goes on last, at the bottom or top, in a solid red with a darker red shadow line inside each loop. Washable tempera covers the large green area faster than markers, and a round brush makes the needle strokes easy. Because the circle sits in the center of the pane, it does block part of the view, so choose a window that is mostly for show.
picks.best_for: Front windows and glass doors that need one clear focal design
picks.skip_if: You need a clear view through that window every day, such as over a kitchen sink
picks.quirky_fact: Painting the needles slightly darker on the lower half of the ring makes a flat wreath look rounded.
picks.product_name: Crayola Premier Tempera Paint, 16 oz, Set of 6

picks.description: A row of ornaments hanging from the top of the frame is quick, colorful and easy to share with children. Draw a few vertical lines of different lengths down from the top edge as strings, then add a circle, teardrop or striped bauble at the end of each. Five to nine ornaments across a standard window looks balanced, and odd numbers read more naturally than even ones. Fill each with a solid color, add a small rectangle cap in gray or gold, and finish with a white curved stroke on one side for shine. Washable window markers handle this design well because the shapes are small, so no brushes are needed. The trade-off is that bright reds and greens can look busy next to an already decorated tree, so keep to two or three colors if the window sits behind your tree.
picks.best_for: Families painting with kids and windows above a sofa or desk
picks.skip_if: The window already frames a lit Christmas tree and you want a calm look
picks.quirky_fact: One short white highlight on each bauble, always on the same side, makes the whole row look lit from one lamp.

picks.description: Hand lettering turns a shop front or front window into a greeting, but it is the design where planning matters most. Decide first who reads it: if it is people outside, the words must be painted backwards on the inside of the glass, which is easiest by taping a reversed printout to the outside and tracing. A script word such as Merry over a bold block word such as Christmas gives contrast without needing two fonts you are unsure of. Paint markers with a medium bullet tip keep letter widths even, and a white or gold outline around red letters helps them read against the dark interior. Keep the lettering in the upper third so it does not compete with anything on the sill. The trade-off is time: getting spacing right takes longer than any other design here, and mistakes are more visible.
picks.best_for: Shop fronts, cafes and street-facing front windows
picks.skip_if: You want a quick project in under half an hour or are painting with small children
picks.quirky_fact: Sign painters usually letter the middle of a word first and work outward, so it stays centered.
picks.product_name: Uni Posca PC-5M Paint Markers, Medium Tip

picks.description: A snowman that seems to lean in from the bottom corner adds humor with very little paint. Only two circles are needed, a large one cut off by the frame and a smaller head above it, plus a carrot nose, coal eyes and a scarf. Because most of the body sits outside the pane, the figure looks like it is peering in, and the empty glass beside it keeps the window usable. Fill the circles with white tempera using a sponge for a soft, snowy texture, then add the details with fine markers once dry. A striped scarf in red and green is the only part that needs care. Keep the snowman to one lower corner and add a few snowflakes above to tie it to the rest of the window. The drawback is that white paint is fairly transparent, so plan on two coats.
picks.best_for: Kitchen windows, kids' bedrooms and glass back doors
picks.skip_if: You prefer an elegant, adult look over playful characters
picks.quirky_fact: Tilting the head circle a little toward the room is what makes the snowman look curious rather than stiff.

picks.breed: Christmas Tree Outline With Dot Lights
picks.description: A tall tree outline is easy to draw and gives a narrow window a strong vertical shape. Mark a star point near the top and two base points near the sill, then join them with a zigzag of three or four tiers, wider at each level. An outline in green or white, rather than a solid fill, keeps the glass mostly clear and is quicker to finish. The detail comes from dot lights: press the tip of a paint marker or the end of a pencil eraser dipped in paint along a draped line, alternating yellow, red and blue. A yellow star on top and a simple pot or gift box at the base complete it. This suits sidelights next to a door where a real tree will not fit. The trade-off is that a lone outline can look sparse on a wide picture window, so pair two trees of different heights there.
picks.best_for: Narrow windows, door sidelights and apartments without room for a real tree
picks.skip_if: Your window is very wide and short, where a tall tree shape looks cramped
picks.quirky_fact: Spacing dot lights about a finger-width apart looks even from the street, even if each dot is slightly different.
picks.product_name: Uni Posca PC-5M Paint Markers, Medium Tip

picks.description: A border of candy canes frames the whole window and leaves the center clear, so it suits windows you look through every day. Draw a row of hooks along the bottom edge, alternating which way they curve, and add a second row up each side if you want a full frame. Paint each cane white first, let it dry, then add diagonal red stripes at the same angle on every cane, which is what makes the border look tidy. Removable stencil vinyl cut into strips can mask straight stripes if freehand lines worry you. A thin green line or a few holly leaves between canes adds variety. The trade-off is that this design takes more paint than it looks, since the white base needs good coverage, and on a large window it can take an hour or more.
picks.best_for: Living room and kitchen windows where the view matters
picks.skip_if: You want something finished in a few minutes or dislike repetitive patterns
picks.quirky_fact: Hooks pointing alternately left and right look intentional, while all facing one way can look like a mistake.
picks.product_name: Oracal 631 Removable Vinyl, White, 12 Inch Roll

picks.description: A painted holly garland swagged across the top of the glass mimics real greenery and pairs well with garland already on the sill or mantel nearby. Lightly sketch a shallow curve or two with chalk marker, then paint pointed holly leaves in pairs along it, varying the angle so they look loose rather than stamped. Two greens, one dark and one brighter, give the leaves depth, and a thin vein line down the middle of each takes seconds with a fine marker. Clusters of three red berries at each dip finish the look. Because the design hugs the top edge, it barely affects light or view. The trade-off is that holly leaves have spiky edges that take practice, so try a few on a sheet of glass from a picture frame first.
picks.best_for: Dining rooms and windows that already have garland on the sill
picks.skip_if: You want a bold design that reads clearly from across the street
picks.quirky_fact: Real holly berries grow in small clusters close to the stem, so tight groups of three look more natural than single dots.
picks.product_name: Crayola Premier Tempera Paint, 16 oz, Set of 6

picks.description: A gingerbread house is the most detailed design here, which makes it a satisfying weekend project for a large lower pane. Draw a simple house front with a pitched roof, a door and two windows, and fill it in a warm brown tempera. The charm comes from the icing: thick white wavy lines along the roof edge and around each window, dots of color for candy buttons and a candy cane or two at the door. A white path and small gingerbread figures can extend the scene sideways if you have room. Liquid chalk markers in white make the icing lines stand out well over brown paint. The drawback is time and layering, since the brown needs to dry fully before the icing goes on, so plan for two sessions.
picks.best_for: Big picture windows, kids' playrooms and cafe or bakery fronts
picks.skip_if: You have only a small window or less than an hour to spend
picks.quirky_fact: Brown tempera looks darker once dry, so mix a slightly lighter shade than you want.
picks.product_name: Chalkola White Liquid Chalk Markers, Fine Tip

picks.description: A poinsettia in one corner adds rich color with a more grown-up feel than cartoon characters. Each bloom is a star of pointed red leaves around a cluster of small yellow dots, so paint five to seven long red petals radiating from a center, then a second, smaller layer between them. Two shades of red, a bright one and a darker one for the inner petals, add depth. A few green leaves behind the bloom anchor it to the corner. Two or three blooms of different sizes in one corner look fuller than a single flower, and the rest of the glass stays clear. Paint markers handle the petal edges well, while tempera covers larger blooms faster. The trade-off is that red can look dark against a bright sky, so outline each petal in white or gold.
picks.best_for: Entryways, front windows and a classic red-and-green color scheme
picks.skip_if: Your room is decorated in silver, blue or neutral tones that red would clash with
picks.quirky_fact: The red parts of a poinsettia are leaves called bracts, and the real flowers are the tiny yellow buds in the middle.
picks.product_name: Uni Posca PC-5M Paint Markers, Medium Tip

faqs.question: What paint is best for Christmas window painting?
faqs.answer: Washable window markers and liquid chalk markers are the least messy and wipe off with a damp cloth. For larger areas, washable tempera paint mixed with a small squeeze of dish soap spreads evenly and lifts off more easily later. Acrylic craft paint is harder to remove from glass and can stain window seals, so save it for practice on a cheap picture frame rather than a rental window.

faqs.question: How do you get window paint off glass?
faqs.answer: Spray the design with warm soapy water and let it sit for a few minutes, then wipe with a microfiber cloth. For stubborn spots, a plastic scraper or an old gift card held flat to the glass lifts dried paint without scratching. Avoid metal blades on tinted or coated windows, and wipe the frame and seals separately so paint does not collect in the corners.

faqs.question: Should I paint the inside or outside of the window?
faqs.answer: Inside is usually better. The paint is protected from rain, frost and condensation that can make tempera run, and you can reach the glass without a ladder. The trade-off is that people outside see the design in reverse, so write any words backwards or use a stencil flipped over. Shop fronts often paint outside so the lettering reads correctly and touch it up after storms.

faqs.question: How do I paint on a window if I can't draw?
faqs.answer: Tape a printed outline to the outside of the glass and trace it from the inside with a white chalk marker, then fill in color. Simple shapes such as circles for ornaments, triangles for trees and six-line snowflakes look neat even when they are not perfect. Removable stencil vinyl cut into stars or snowflakes also gives clean edges.

faqs.question: Can kids do Christmas window painting?
faqs.answer: Yes, with washable window markers or tempera and a towel along the sill. Give younger children the lower panes and simple shapes such as ornaments or snowflakes, and handle lettering and outlines yourself. Washable products are the safer choice in homes with small children, and they are much easier to clean if paint lands on the frame or floor.

seo_title: Christmas Window Painting Ideas 2026: 10 Easy Designs
answer: The easiest Christmas window paintings are snowflake corner clusters, a painted wreath with a red bow and a row of hanging ornaments. The deciding factor is paint: use washable window markers or tempera mixed with a drop of dish soap so the design wipes off cleanly in January.
method: Picked from Pinterest's trending searches for Christmas window painting ideas, then ordered by how easy each design is for a beginner, how well it reads from a distance and how cleanly it comes off.
author: Elena Marsh
